passage: The last bell had gone and the corridor was noisy with chairs and shoes. Zeenat stayed at her desk with her failed spelling paper, expecting to feel worse than ever. Ms Dilnaz pulled a chair beside her. "Let's look at this together. See here, you wrote 'recieve'? The rule is i before e, except after c." She circled the word gently. Zeenat's eyes prickled. Nobody had ever stayed after school for her. They went through four more words, and Ms Dilnaz asked her to spell them aloud. At the door Ms Dilnaz said, "I think you'll do better on the next one." Zeenat walked home feeling lighter.

qa.q: What word did Zeenat spell wrongly that Ms Dilnaz pointed out?
qa.a: She wrote 'recieve' instead of the correct spelling.

qa.q: What was Zeenat feeling when her eyes prickled?
qa.a: Touched and cared for, because nobody had ever stayed after school just for her.

qa.q: Why is accepting Ms Dilnaz's help not a weakness for Zeenat?
qa.a: It shows that someone believes she can improve, and going through the mistakes together turns the failed paper into something she can fix. 🙂

qa.q: What might Ms Dilnaz be thinking when she says she thinks Zeenat will do better?
qa.a: She believes Zeenat can improve, and wants her to know it.

grounding: A child failing a test is cared for by a teacher who stays back to explain the mistakes.

passage:
The spelling test came back to Wanjiru with a big 4/20 in the corner. It was her second term in Oslo, and Norwegian words still tangled on her tongue. She folded the paper small.
When the bell rang, Ms. Ulla said, "Wanjiru, can you stay five minutes?" Wanjiru's stomach dropped.
But Ms. Ulla pulled a chair up beside her and unfolded the paper gently. "Look, most mistakes are the same kind: letters that sound different from English. That's normal. Let's make a little list of those, and I'll check it with you every Tuesday."
They worked until the cleaner came in. Walking to the bus, Wanjiru realised she wasn't embarrassed any more. Ms. Ulla had stayed because she thought Wanjiru could do it.

qa.q: What score did Wanjiru get in the spelling test?
How did Wanjiru feel walking to the bus?
qa.a: No longer embarrassed; she felt cared for and believed in.

qa.q: What made Ms. Ulla's help effective?
qa.a: She found the pattern in the mistakes, made a small list and set regular Tuesday checks.

qa.q: How does Ms. Ulla see Wanjiru's low score?
qa.a: As a normal stage in learning a new language, not a sign that Wanjiru cannot do it.

grounding: A girl whose teacher stays back to explain her mistakes feels cared for and sees that accepting help means someone believes she can improve.

passage:
The staff room was empty except for Irawati Ma'am and a pile of notebooks. She had asked Bidisha to come after school with her failed geometry paper.
Bidisha dragged her feet. Only the weak kids got called for extra help, she thought. What if someone saw?
Irawati Ma'am cleared a space. "Show me number six. Tell me what you were thinking." Bidisha explained, stumbling. Ma'am nodded. "Your thinking was right until here. You forgot that angles on a straight line add up to 180. That's all."
They did three more together. On the third, Bidisha got it before Ma'am spoke.
"You see?" Ma'am smiled. "I don't stay back for students I've given up on."
Bidisha walked out warm-faced, but not from embarrassment.

qa.q: Which question did Irawati Ma'am ask to see first?
Why did Bidisha drag her feet to the staff room?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed, thinking only weak students got extra help, and worried someone would see.

qa.q: How did Irawati Ma'am help Bidisha learn from the mistake?
qa.a: She asked Bidisha to explain her thinking, pinpointed the one forgotten rule and practised three more with her.

qa.q: What does staying back mean to Irawati Ma'am?
qa.a: It shows she believes the student can improve; she does not stay back for students she has given up on.

grounding: A girl ashamed to need extra help finds her teacher's time after school means the teacher believes she can improve.
